current_tasks: SHIPPED - the run says which workspace it is for. A four-degree ladder in `refarm ask`: explicit --workspace (recorded `declared`) > the session's own stored declaration (inherited) > a cwd seed at session creation (recorded `seeded-from-cwd`) > nothing. One resolved value travels twice by design -- Effort.workspaceId to the sidecar for refarm.workspace.id, args.workspace_id to the agent, which stamps the Session node so later runs inherit. cwd is ABSENT from the dispatch-time order (ADR-094 D2) and acts once, at session birth, writing a declaration stamped with its provenance (H2). A read failure of the stored declaration is `unknown`, NOT `unattributed` -- collapsing those two would silently re-attribute an established conversation from wherever the operator happens to stand. LIVE: seed -> `refarm`, declaration -> `rcdc5`, and a flag-less follow-up from a directory seeding `refarm` still recorded `rcdc5`. Coverage 2/23 -> 8/29.

SHIPPED - the declaration reaches the path a real ask takes. The first live proof FAILED on inheritance and that failure was the point: reported honestly, it exposed TWO broken links, which is why every function looked correct in isolation. (1) A `refarm ask` never reaches execute_respond -- the sidecar fires the prompt as a reply-less EventEnvelope::fire("user:prompt"), so the runner takes call_on_event -> handle_prompt, and the EnvGuards sat on a real but different path. (2) Upstream, dispatch.rs::extract_task_args had no workspace_id field at all, so the payload never carried the declaration. The regression test drives the real user:prompt path against the real agent.wasm and was PROVEN to fail against the pre-fix binary; clean_model_env gained both vars so a leaked environment cannot forge a pass.

SHIPPED - the record can say a run was WRONG. refarm.verification.expected/.passed/.method/.unknown, with refarm.outcome untouched: `done` still means the run completed, and correctness is a separate fact. Three states are STRUCTURAL (Matched | NotMatched | Unverifiable(reason), no Absent variant), so an expectation declared but not comparable can never be recorded as a failure. `refarm ask --expect <text>`, substring match, method recorded beside the verdict. Proven live: expect 59 -> passed, expect 9999 -> failed, outcome `done` in both.

SHIPPED - the step fraction, and the 4/25 mystery is solved. steps_completed/steps_planned now count the SAME notion (completion-loop steps) and match the `step N/M` the sidecar prints; the turn count survives as refarm.outcome.turns_completed and travels ALONE, never as half a fraction. Why it looked impossible: a turn is a DISPATCH (one refarm ask = one turn) and nothing declares a max number of turns, so a turn count genuinely has no denominator -- the observation concluded, reasonably and wrongly, that only an AgentPlan could supply one. The 25 was never a plan; it is the react loop's own ceiling, and it always rode on prompt_ref, the same key the observation joins on. A second real off-by-one was found underneath: the loop ran 0..=max_iter, so a ceiling of 25 made 26 completions and would have recorded 26/25. BEHAVIOUR CHANGE: MODEL_TOOL_CALL_MAX_ITER=N now makes N completions per dispatch, not N+1.

SHIPPED - work is comparable. refarm.scenario.id (declared, never invented) and .hash (derived from the request shape at dispatch, canonicalised, key-order-stable). Two exclusions were found by MEASURING rather than reasoning: args.replyRef and args.session_id are per-run identifiers, and leaving either in made every run hash uniquely. A fact that is NOT a defect and must not be 'fixed': an agent request is never identical to itself, because ask's system prompt is assembled with DateContextProvider and GitStatusContextProvider. So grouping on the agent path comes from the DECLARED id -- `refarm ask --scenario X` -- not from the hash.

blockers: OPERATIONAL DEFECT 1 -- `refarm budget observations` goes blind, and it is the command this work exists to serve. storage/sqlite.rs:188 has NO ORDER BY at all, and both readers take from the front: sidecar/mod.rs:1590 does .take(limit.min(100)) and host/wasi_bridge/core.rs:382 does .take(limit). So it returns the OLDEST N, and past 100 observations it can never surface a recent one at ANY --limit. currentRateTableFrom (budget.ts:379), documented as derived from the NEWEST observation, derives from the oldest. The same unordered take hits latest_session_id(20)/latest_session_leaf_id(10) in wasm_ops.rs:59-76, which pick the newest among the OLDEST N sessions. The record is at 29 today.

OPERATIONAL DEFECT 2 -- `refarm doctor --json` reported CLEAN while the daemon ran 9-hour-stale code, twice, observed independently by two agents on 2026-08-05, verified by hand with sha256. The `runtime:stale` finding this handoff records as SHIPPED did not fire. A gate that reports clean over stale code is a lying instrument, and it cost two agents a wrong diagnosis inside a single plan. A false entry in the durable record is worse than a missing one.

OPERATIONAL DEFECT 3 -- `cargo component build --release` does NOT republish packages/agent/dist/agent.wasm, which is what `refarm plugin install` reads. The documented build command silently leaves stale code installed. Working path: `pnpm --filter @refarm.dev/agent run build` -> `refarm plugin install` -> `refarm runtime restart`. Defect 2 is what makes this silent; with a working staleness check this one is loud.

open_questions: Should the budget record cover work refarm did not dispatch? The workspace-attribution plan itself cost ~1.5M subagent tokens across 17 dispatches, and NONE of it is in the BudgetObservation record -- that record covers `refarm ask` dispatches, not other tools. The operator's stated goal is to account for everything. Either refarm accepts observations from outside over a wire contract, or it admits it measures only what it dispatches. The answer shapes the fourth axis too.

Does the bench need a correctness axis richer than substring? `--expect` grades work whose answer is checkable that way and nothing else. An automation with a known expected result is a scenario WITH a grader, which is the cheap path; a judge model is the expensive one. Neither is built.

Where does a NODE-scoped automation live? .project/automations.json is project-scoped and the governed writer says so in its name. Two of the three known customers -- restarting this node, verifying this node's catalog -- are node concerns. The sovereign dir is the obvious home, beside config.json, node.json and model-rates.v1.json.

Which cron parser? None exists, this repo is deliberately dependency-light, and cron is subtly easy to get wrong (day-of-week versus day-of-month). Vendoring something tested likely beats hand-rolling, and the choice deserves the same source-and-date discipline every other external dependency here now carries.

rcdc5 as a workspace-scoped automation consumer is BLOCKED on two named pieces, and the blocker is a declared principle rather than an oversight: pending_prompt.rs states P1, `a pending prompt's lifetime is its asker's lifetime, nothing persists`, and nothing resumes a persisted non-terminal effort. Until both change, an automation that waits for an MFA push cannot survive a restart, and 'waiting for a human' is indistinguishable from 'dead'.
